comments.author: teaearlgraycold
comments.text: I love how good local models are and how optimized the software is. I was gifted a couple of old workstation cards (Turing generation RTX 6000s) and put them to use hosting Qwen 3.8 27B. With llama.cpp I can split the weights across the cards so they run in parallel. Multiple requests can batch together. I get 60 tok/s for one request or 40 tok/s each for two concurrent requests. And the model’s way smarter than it should be given the size. In a few years new mid-range consumer hardware will actually be hosting models that are worth running.

comments.text:

Wow.  Nice gift!

As a happy contrast to the whole 'giant companies holding the economy hostage and growing a huge bubble' downside (to put it mildly) the increasing capability and availability of locally hosted AI on, admittedly expensive (but not unreachably fiscally inaccessible) hardware, is very nice and puts tools and capabilities in the hands of the individual instead of megacorps looking to go further down the 'you'll own nothing, pay a subscription for everything, and thank us for it' path.

comments.author: ThrowdoBaggins
comments.text:
admittedly expensive (but not unreachably fiscally inaccessible) hardware


I’ve been trying to think of a way to explain this to my family (who don’t really pay attention to AI stuff except that it’s on their work computers everywhere now) and I phrased it as “incredibly expensive consumer-grade, or surprisingly cheap business-grade kinds of prices” — which I think feels about right?

If I look at a colour laser printer, for example, I can get decent quality consumer grade version for well under $1000, but as soon as I’m looking at a commercial product, that’s instantly looking at about an order of magnitude higher.

Spending $10k-20k on a home computer seems like incredibly dedicated hobbyist kinds of prices, but for a small business that’s ... okay it’s not easy, but certainly more achievable, especially if it’s a tool you need for your business.

comments.author: teaearlgraycold
comments.text:
I have a server with those RTX 6000s in it. Yesterday I vibe-coded an agent that can access an organization's mediawiki website as well as search the accompanying Discord server. It can respond in Discord channels and DMs citing wiki pages and Discord messages. It can also review your memes since I added the vision part of the model. The hardware necessary to run it would be ~$2500. It's actually pretty useful because you can have it summarize tremendously long arguments between people instead of needing to dig through 10,000 words yourself.

Normally I'd find something like this kind of gross, but because it's 100% self-hosted and has no write access (outside of message replies), no memories or other persistent state, and operates within our k8s cluster where the wiki is it's something I'm happy to have around.

comments.author: skybrian
comments.text:
From the article:



AI has gotten cheaper more quickly than any other transformative technology in history. The cost of achieving a given level of AI performance has fallen about 47% per quarter since 2023, or 13× per year. That price drop is four times faster than DNA sequencing, six times faster than compute, 18 times faster than lithium batteries, and (in the century up to 1973) 54 times faster than electricity.



[...]


The next chart shows some examples. On January 31, 2025, OpenAI released a new iteration in its series of “reasoning” models, called o3. We estimate that for an average cost of 30 cents per question, it could achieve a 75% score on GPQA Diamond, a multiple-choice exam covering PhD-level physics, chemistry, and biology.1 Just under 18 months later, OpenAI released GPT-5.6 Luna. It scored just as well — for four hundredths of a penny per question ($0.0004). That is a 725-fold drop in the price of thought in under 18 months. It is like the sticker price on a new car falling from $50,000 to $69. No other general-purpose technology in history appears to have gotten so cheap so fast.


[...]


Our analysis comes with major caveats. AI companies may be expressly training their models for some benchmarks (“benchmaxxing”), so that improvement on the benchmarks outstrips improvement for real-world tasks. Even if they are not, doing well on a benchmark is not synonymous with useful work. Because we focus on the frontier — the absolute cheapest model capable of any given level of performance — we implicitly posit an AI user who relentlessly searches for the most cost-effective model for each task, when real users do not switch models so often, and therefore do not reap quite the same savings. Our data are incomplete and noisy: the timeframe is barely three years, and we do not include all combinations of AI model and benchmark. Prices drop differently for different models, benchmarks, time periods, and performance ranges, and there are many reasonable ways to average over this variegated experience. Overall, while we believe that our bottom-line numbers are reasonably representative of reality, they should not be read as exact.
